article.title: Effective Altruism Is Increasingly Just Funding Itself
article.author: Jacob Davis
article.content: The basic pitch for effective altruism (EA) is simple: charitable giving is an investment, whose return is in others’ well-being rather than your financial betterment. Given that it’s an investment, it makes sense to look for a strong, measurable return from wherever you choose to donate. After all, if you really care about others being well-off, you should be at least as conscientious about these investments as you are about your retirement savings. This is, to say the least, a controversial approach to charity. It has many detractors: those who argue that the approach flattens value to numbers in a spreadsheet, or that it ignores the place of solidarity and political organizing. But the ethic also has its undeniable appeal. Among effective altruists, the standard example of effective giving is usually the Against Malaria Foundation (AMF), which distributes insecticide-laced bed nets in sub-Saharan Africa to combat mosquito-borne illness. It is hard to argue that AMF is not a better place to give your money than many competing organizations, like various sketchy “ voluntourism ” outfits or microloan creditors . Where many critiques of EA miss the mark is in taking this pitch at face value. In reality, as measured by volume of money flow, EA is more a means of cultivating a self-selecting, insular subculture based around the tech industry. The biggest objection that can be laid against it is not that its founding principles are misguided, but that they have come to play third or fourth fiddle to building a playground and safety net for a small, privileged portion of the global population. Short-Term vs. Long-Term EA Within EA, a distinction is sometimes drawn between “long-term” and “short-term” effective altruism. Classic poster children like AMF almost all fall on the “short-term” side of the split: concrete, clearly specifiable interventions to promote measurable goods in the present or near future. “Long-term” cause areas are generally more nebulous or speculative: preparations for future pandemics, the eventual curtailment of wild animal suffering, or (above all) artificial intelligence safety. Long-term cause areas generally, and AI safety specifically, have come to dominate EA organizing. One measure of this is the recent spending decisions of Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), the dominant EA grant-making body. In 2025 , nearly $490 million of Coefficient Giving’s roughly $840 million in grants were dedicated to “long-term and existential risk,” overwhelmingly in AI safety. This is in contrast to the approximately $150 million spent on global health and development, the classic “short-term” general cause area. This spending strategy is puzzling, under traditional EA principles. As Coefficient Giving states on its funding page, effective altruists deliberately focus on funding for problems that are important , neglected , and tractable . Without prejudice to the issue’s importance, there is a growing consensus among concerned parties that AI safety is not currently tractable: there is widespread recognition that no robust technical road map to safe AI has been, or will likely soon be, forthcoming. And leading AI safety organization Anthropic just opened its initial public offering (IPO) at around $1.5 trillion — prompting disillusionment even within EA. Rarely in human history has any problem been less economically neglected. Anthropic, like OpenAI before it, highlights the double-edged nature of much technical AI safety research. In the eyes of most effective altruists, developing AI capabilities is directly opposed to the goal of AI safety. And yet most avenues of technical safety research go hand-in-hand with capabilities development; indeed, this is a criticism lobbed against AI safety initiatives by many effective altruists. Research projects on interpretability , reinforcement learning with human feedback, and thinking traces have all failed to realize the elusive dream of AI “alignment” but have provided considerable returns to sheer performance levels. What AI safety funding does offer is an opportunity to spread money around a self-selecting community of EA researchers and activists. A dizzying number of conferences, think tanks, and fellowships have sprung up to study the topic, backed by funders like Coefficient Giving. Much as a liberal-interventionist foreign policy makes for “ a full-employment strategy for the foreign policy establishment,” so the focus on AI safety provides the AI safety community abundant opportunity for remunerative work and stimulating play. Effective Altruism for Profit Perhaps no organization better illustrates these tendencies than Manifund , a San Francisco–based fundraising body closely tied to the EA community. Whereas Coefficient Giving has historically acted mainly as a channel for the philanthropy of billionaire couple Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna, Manifund is designed to invite funding from a range of interested onlookers. Much of this fundraising is conducted through Manifund’s “impact certificate ecosystem,” which they describe as “ like Kickstarter meets the stock market .” The organization also subscribes to a principle of full transparency, making its grant-making process unusually accessible. Many of its grant choices are atypical, to say the least. In a recent blog post, for example, Manifund CEO and cofounder Austin Chen explains a number of routes the organization uses to funnel donor money into for-profit ventures — in spite of Manifund’s status as a 501(c)3 tax-exempt non-profit. These range from the relatively innocuous (commissions for specific services) to the legal but abnormal (outright investment). Manifund has adopted more indirect means of supporting for-profit entities, as well. For example, it is responsible for funding and running Mox , an EA workspace and community hub in Downtown San Francisco. In addition to offering work space for individual paying members, Mox — which shares Chen as head — plays host to several EA-affiliated small businesses. And this summer, Mox and Manifund co-organized Surplus , a software start-up incubator offering generous seed funding and pitch opportunities to successful applicants. Similarly unorthodox have been the charity’s recent hiring decisions. Against considerable uproar, Manifund recently hired effective altruist and convicted fraudster Caroline Ellison to serve on its administrative staff. In 2024, Ellison was sentenced to two years’ incarceration in connection with her roles at cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research and sister company FTX. She has since July played a major role alongside Chen in approving and directing grant decisions at Manifund, as well as contributing to the charity’s Substack. This decision prompted considerable backlash from the EA community. Complaints stemmed partly from concerns about optics, given the extremely negative attention Ellison had already attracted to EA. But there were also more direct concerns about her trustworthiness and competence, especially in a financially responsible role, as well as resentment from victims of fraud connected to FTX and Alameda Research. Chen defended the decision in the September blog post announcing the hire, offering among other reasons a sense of indebtedness to FTX: I felt a keen debt to the FTX Future Fund. They provided seed funding for Manifold. They funded the retreat which drew me into the EA community, and the conference where I met my wife. Much of Manifund’s work today is directly inspired by the Future Fund’s approach . The Future Fund was the philanthropic wing of FTX, which at the time was linked to fraudulently acquired funds siphoned from the exchange’s account holders. In addition to Manifund, the Future Fund supported a number of EA-related causes, primarily related to AI safety and pandemic prevention. The Transfer of Wealth In all of these capacities, Manifund has consistently deprioritized “short-term” EA work of the sort exemplified by AMF. Often, this has been in favour of recognizable “long-term” cause areas, like AI safety. But sometimes its beneficiaries have not even clearly fit this more extensive mold and instead have been connected to EA more through cultural and ideological affinity. An easy indication of this is the official breakdown of Manifund grants by cause area. Best-funded is “ Technical AI Safety ” at over $8 million, coming out ahead of similarly AI-dominated causes like “ AI Governance ” ($5.2 million) and “ Global Catastrophic Risks ” ($4.7 million). All of these come out ahead of “ Global Health and Development ,” which clocks in at a comparatively meagre $436,000. (Cause areas are not mutually exclusive, so some of these funding amounts overlap.) The immediate net effect of this outsize investment in technical AI safety is a transfer of wealth to the EA-dominated AI safety research community. Existing technical AI safety initiatives are effectively all research- or education-oriented: given the lack of any widely recognized way of implementing AI safety, the main place for funding to go is to researchers either currently trying to develop strategies for AI safety or learning what is needed to do the same. EA-affiliated AI governance initiatives, in turn, are carried out in close coordination with technical researchers and draw from a similar subcultural pool. Many non-AI projects with heavy support from Manifund similarly circulate the EA cash pool among other effective altruists. For example, Manifund has raised $132,000 in funding for “ human intelligence amplification @ Berkeley Genomics Project” — an attempt to breed a new generation of hyperintelligent humans through genomic engineering, in the hopes that they may be better suited to design safe AI systems. Setting aside any ethical considerations, the project is unlikely to generate immediate fruit. Rather, the main immediate impact is the opportunity to conduct highly speculative bioengineering research much in vogue among effective altruists. The same tendency is even more directly on display in the “ EA Community ” category ($1.6 million). Best-funded of all projects in the category, after Mox, is Lightcone Infrastructure — the common funding and governing body of LessWrong and the EA hotel turned event venue Lighthaven. Lighthaven, acquired by Lightcone in 2022 ( reportedly with the substantial financial assistance of FTX), has subsequently hosted a number of conferences, programs, and parties associated with the EA community in the Bay Area. More indirect support from Manifund, such as through Mox, continues this trend. Some of the start-ups using Mox’s office space, for example, are only very dubiously philanthropic ventures. They include The Relationship Company (a dating app “making AI systems that understand who you are and find people you’d genuinely connect with”) and Stardrift (an AI-based travel agency). Expanding the Circle A common metaphor used to explain EA to outsiders is the “ circle of concern .” Moral progress, in this story, is largely a matter of expanding this “circle:” the range of people, animals, and things about which one cares. At the center of your circle is you, whom you will care about even if you are maximally greedy and selfish. Beyond that lie family, neighbors, countrymen, humanity writ large, and the animal kingdom, at ever wider removes. Effective altruism, at its best, is about maintaining a wide circle of concern, in a self-consciously rational way. The irony in this tale is that EA has often had the opposite effect. Where charitable donations might otherwise have gone to distant victims of poverty, illness, and disaster, many EA organizations have instead channeled them primarily to one another. Rather than expanding its devotees’ circle of concern, effective altruism has come to consist largely in narrowing that circle to effective altruists.
